title: How Closed Airspace Threatens U.S. Military Mobility Across Eurasia
gist: Former AirBridgeCargo insider Alex Kolbin argues that Russian airspace closures since 2022 and the 2026 Iran war have made Eurasian aviation disruptions asymmetric, persistent and cumulative, concentrating traffic into shrinking corridors (Caucasus, Gulf) and turning scarce widebody freighters into geopolitical assets. Because US military mobility depends on this civilian ecosystem, the Pentagon should treat contested mobility as a network-resilience problem, not just a matter of owning 275 strategic airlifters.

insights.claim: Post-2022 Eurasian aviation disruptions differ from COVID because they are asymmetric (airlines have different political access to the same geography), persistent (restrictions outlast the shock), and cumulative (losing one route increases dependence on what remains).
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Route-access risk is now a structural, not cyclical, factor for airlines, air cargo and logistics valuations.
insights.quote: they are asymmetric, persistent, and cumulative
insights.locator: The disruptions accumulating in Eurasia since 2022

insights.claim: Chinese airlines, which retained Russian airspace access, rose from about 55 percent of scheduled China–Europe capacity in summer 2019 to 83 percent by summer 2025 while total market capacity stayed flat.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Political airspace access became a commercial moat for Chinese carriers at the expense of European airlines on China–Europe routes.

insights.claim: After losing Russian airspace, Finnair's Helsinki–Tokyo flight time rose from about nine to 13 hours (a 44 percent increase), and during the latest Middle East disruption airlines rerouted 1,150 flights per day, adding 206,000 kilometers daily.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Longer routings raise fuel burn and costs for Western carriers — a persistent margin headwind and a support for jet fuel demand.

insights.claim: Kyiv has asked ICAO to treat Russian airspace as unsafe due to Ukrainian drone operations, EASA recommends against operating in Russian airspace west of 60 degrees east, and suspected Russian sabotage and GPS jamming have reached Leipzig/Halle and the Baltic Sea.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: European logistics hubs themselves are now contested, raising operational and insurance risk for European air cargo.
insights.locator: Moreover, the problem is now escalating

insights.claim: In summer 2025 EUROCONTROL estimated it controlled only about 80 percent of the airspace available before Russia's invasion of Ukraine, with Russian-origin radio-frequency interference adding further disruption.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Structural capacity loss in European airspace compounds congestion and delay costs for European carriers.

insights.claim: With Russian airspace to the north and Iranian and Gulf airspace to the south disrupted, east-west traffic at one point narrowed to a corridor of roughly 160 kilometers, with Georgia, Azerbaijan, Armenia and Turkey absorbing much of the flow.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Single-corridor concentration creates chokepoint risk; a Caucasus disruption would sharply hit Eurasian air logistics.

insights.claim: Azerbaijan's air navigation system went from about 278 flights a day in early 2022 to 695 by end-2025, and annual overflights rose from 47,065 in 2021 to 261,085 in 2025, rising further after Gulf airspace disruption in early 2026.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Azerbaijan is a major beneficiary (overflight revenues, hub role) of Eurasian rerouting — and a new single point of failure given Azerbaijan–Armenia tensions.
insights.locator: Developments in the Caucasus since 2022

insights.claim: Dubai handled a record 95.2 million passengers in 2025 as the Gulf became the key east-west bridge, but the 2026 Iran war cut Dubai's first-half 2026 passengers 31.3 percent year on year to 31.5 million and aircraft movements 32.1 percent.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Gulf hub carriers and airports took a severe 2026 hit; their post-2022 bridge advantage is exposed to Iran-related conflict risk.
insights.locator: The Gulf shows the same concentration.

insights.claim: On March 31, 2026, EUROCONTROL recorded 56 percent fewer flights between the Middle East and Europe, showing that a second loss of geography is more consequential after the first removed an alternative.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Compounding route losses produce nonlinear disruption to air travel and cargo — tail risk for airlines and time-sensitive supply chains.
insights.locator: Then the Gulf itself was hit.

insights.claim: Smaller shocks — Israel-related tensions emptying Eastern Mediterranean routes, the May 2025 India–Pakistan confrontation pushing traffic toward Oman and the Gulf, and activity around Korea and Taiwan — further consume the alternatives the Eurasian network depends on.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Multiple regional flashpoints jointly erode airline routing flexibility, raising correlated disruption risk.
insights.locator: Smaller disruptions only compound the same problem.

themes.theme: US military mobility depends on civil aviation

insights.claim: US global military mobility was built inside the civilian aviation ecosystem — commercial airlines, airports, cargo hubs, maintenance, fuel and accessible airspace — which the Pentagon never had to own to benefit from.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Fragmentation of civil aviation directly degrades US power projection, raising the strategic value of US cargo airlines and allied hubs.

insights.claim: Via the Northern Distribution Network from 2009, the US relied on Russian geography and Russian airlift for Afghanistan: Volga-Dnepr An-124s flew NATO missions and by April 2011 over 1,000 US supply missions transited Russian airspace carrying more than 150,000 personnel.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Shows how much former US mobility leaned on now-hostile Russian assets and geography.
insights.locator: Afghanistan demonstrated how far that interdependency

insights.claim: US Transportation Command's organic fleet is 52 C-5Ms and 223 C-17s matching a validated 275-aircraft requirement, but CRS notes the Air Force operates 222 C-17s after a hull loss and one belongs to NATO's Strategic Airlift Capability, so usable fleet is already below the paper figure.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: US strategic airlift is already short of its validated requirement, supporting demand for airlift recapitalization.

insights.claim: The Civil Reserve Air Fleet can augment lift but cannot create overflight rights, accessible airports or acceptable corridors; participating airlines keep operational control and can refuse missions on risk grounds, as in the 2021 Afghanistan evacuation where 18 activated CRAF aircraft did not fly into Kabul.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Commercial airlift surge capacity is limited by political access and airline risk appetite in high-threat scenarios.

insights.claim: US Transportation Command's May 2024 Unsuitable Vendor List included Air China Cargo, China Eastern and China Southern alongside Russian-origin carriers, yet CRAF carriers Delta and United still maintain codeshares with China Eastern and Air China respectively.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Possible future pressure on US airline–Chinese carrier partnerships as strategic vetting tightens.
insights.locator: That ecosystem is becoming more politically constrained

insights.claim: Ahead of the February 2026 Iran war, the US moved about 150 aircraft into Europe and the Middle East with over half based in Europe beyond Iranian missile range, and KC-135 tankers from Europe refueled B-1s over CENTCOM.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: European bases are integral to Middle East operations, making allied political access a key operational variable.
insights.locator: The military network adapted to the same geography.

insights.claim: Spain denied its airspace and bases to US aircraft supporting attacks on Iran, forcing fifteen US aircraft, mostly KC-135 tankers, out of Rota and Morón, with at least seven moving to Ramstein — an allied, issue-specific and more reversible form of access denial.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Even NATO allies can withhold access; raises the strategic value of Germany and other compliant hosts.

themes.theme: Widebody freighters as scarce geopolitical assets

insights.claim: Boeing ended C-17 production in 2015 and delivered the final 747 in 2023, and the An-124 fleet is limited, so the most useful widebody airlift is finite and hard to replace while demand rises.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Scarcity supports freighter lease rates and the value of existing 747 freighter fleets and operators like Atlas Air.
insights.locator: Scarcity adds another layer.

insights.claim: In 2025, more than two-thirds of the value of global trade in AI-related goods moved by air, and some AI server racks are so large they increasingly require 747 freighter capabilities such as the nose cargo door.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: AI hardware buildout is a demand driver for scarce 747 freighter capacity — bullish for 747 operators, competing with military lift.
insights.quote: more than two-thirds of the value of global trade in AI-related goods moved by air
insights.locator: Scarcity adds another layer.

insights.claim: Atlas Air, Kalitta Air and National Airlines (all CRAF participants) have flown 747 freighters under US defense contracts carrying weapons to Europe for Ukraine while serving disrupted global trade, so immobilizing part of the fleet removes capacity from all users.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Military and commercial demand compete for the same freighters, tightening air cargo capacity.

insights.claim: More than a dozen AirBridgeCargo 747-8 freighters have sat at Moscow's Sheremetyevo since 2022 and Western lessors recovered none, even though the fleet's ~1 million tons of annual prewar capacity dwarfed Russia's entire ~150,000-ton international air cargo market.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Western lessors face persistent write-offs on Russia-trapped aircraft; global freighter supply is effectively reduced.

insights.claim: Bank of China-controlled BOC Aviation won a $406.2 million judgment against AirBridgeCargo and, months after Putin's October 2023 Beijing visit, Russia let its two 747-8 freighters leave in March 2024 — which Western lessors could not achieve — and Atlas Air later put them into US service.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Asset recovery from Russia depends on lessor nationality — Chinese lessors hold a geopolitical advantage.

insights.claim: A September 2026 EU-funded strategic airlift study identified two options for Europe's outsized cargo capacity: deep modernization of Ukrainian An-124s or developing a new European aircraft to replace the C-17.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Potential European defense-aerospace program opportunity (Airbus or Antonov modernization) to watch.

insights.claim: Chinese carriers exploiting trans-Siberian airspace still depend on American-built freighters: nearly 60 Boeing 777 freighters are operated by six Chinese carriers and SF Airlines relies entirely on Boeing types.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: China's air cargo advantage rests on US aircraft and support — a lever in US-China trade relations.
insights.locator: China illustrates another asymmetry.

insights.claim: China agreed in 2026 to a prospective 200-aircraft Boeing package within US–China trade negotiations while also diversifying, with Air China Cargo ordering 10 Airbus A350 freighters.
insights.speaker: Alex Kolbin
insights.so_what: Boeing order flow from China is tied to trade diplomacy; Airbus gains share as China hedges.

insights.so_what: Effective US airlift capacity is likely overstated by fleet counts — a blind spot in force planning.
